result: The mean frequency of LFPs recorded in the stratum radiatum of CA1 was 45.2 ± 1.2 Hz (n = 7 animals), corresponding to the low-gamma frequency band that characterizes the hippocampal CA3-CA1 segment.
evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 are well-supported by direct experimental measurements using autocorrelation analysis on 10-minute epochs from 7 animals, with appropriate citations to previous literature establishing this frequency range as low-gamma in the hippocampus. The methodology is clearly described and the sample size is adequate.

result: Schaffer activity shows significant wide-band coherence within ipsilateral antero-posterior sites (0.5 mm apart) but reduced coherence restricted to gamma band in bilateral comparisons. Cross-correlation coefficients were higher for ipsilateral (La-Lp: 0.84 ± 0.03) than bilateral (Ra-La: 0.57 ± 0.04) comparisons (F(1,12) = 26.9; p<0.001), with the right side leading by -0.82 ± 0.3 ms (F(1,12) = 8.5, p=0.01).
evaluation: Claims C23-C29 provide converging quantitative evidence from coherence and cross-correlation analyses showing stronger ipsilateral than bilateral synchronization, with right-side precedence. The statistical tests are appropriate (F-tests with adequate degrees of freedom), sample size is stated (n=7), and the findings are internally consistent across multiple analytical approaches.

result: Individual gamma waves show high amplitude and duration covariance along ipsilateral lamellar strips (ρA = 0.78 ± 0.02, ρD = 0.63 ± 0.02 for La:Lp) but lower bilateral covariance (ρA = 0.5 ± 0.04, ρD = 0.44 ± 0.03 for La-Ra). Wave duration was identical bilaterally (26.7 ± 0.7 ms; F(1,12) = 0, p=0.96), but right-side waves were significantly larger in amplitude (Ra: 299 ± 11 µV; La: 237 ± 15 µV; F(1,12) = 12, p=0.005).
evaluation: Claims C30-C33 present detailed quantitative analysis of individual gamma wave features using a novel deconvolution method. The statistical comparisons are appropriate with adequate sample size (n=7 animals), and the findings reveal important bilateral asymmetries. The methodology for wave extraction is described in detail in the Methods section.

result: Bilateral waves were rarely initiated synchronously, with right-side waves leading more frequently (55.6 ± 0.8% vs 44.4 ± 0.8%) by similar lags at anterior and posterior sites (Ra-La: 0.62 ± 0.14 ms; Rp-Lp: 0.67 ± 0.18 ms). Unilateral waves occurred more frequently on the right (R: 11.7 ± 2.4%; L: 5.5 ± 1%) and were smaller than bilateral waves in the right hemisphere (212 ± 20 µV; p=0.002) but not the left (192 ± 20 µV; p=0.09).
evaluation: Claims C34-C39 provide detailed temporal analysis of bilateral wave relationships showing consistent right-side dominance. The quantitative measurements are precise, statistical tests are appropriate, and the findings are internally consistent. The presence of unilateral waves provides important evidence for independent bilateral generators.

result: Granger Causality analysis confirmed statistically significant reciprocal relations between right and left Schaffer activities (p=10⁻⁶ and p=10⁻⁸ for L to R and R to L, respectively), with the functional relation peaking in low-gamma (30-50 Hz) and right-to-left dominance. Phase analysis revealed a mean lag of Δϕ = 0.22 ± 0.04 radians (Δt = 0.95 ± 0.2 ms) in one experiment, with population mean of Δϕ = 0.12 ± 0.06 radians (Δt = 0.54 ± 0.26 ms) across all seven animals.
evaluation: Claims C40-C44 employ sophisticated analytical methods (Granger Causality and phase analysis) that converge on consistent findings of right-to-left directionality. The statistical significance is strong, and the time lags are consistent with those obtained from paired wave analysis, providing cross-validation of the findings.

result: The right-left lag was accentuated when R-waves were longer (a, p: 3.09 ± 0.06 and 3.03 ± 0.17 ms), while longer L-waves led right-hand ones by a smaller amount (a, p: 1.97 ± 0.13 and 1.91 ± 0.23 ms, F(1,12) = 517, p<0.001). There was a general tendency for longer and larger waves to lead irrespective of side.
evaluation: Claims C45-C47 reveal important relationships between wave features and timing, showing that wave duration influences bilateral lag patterns. The statistical significance is very strong (F(1,12) = 517, p<0.001), and the findings suggest complex dynamics beyond simple unidirectional driving.

result: The minimum time for CA3 spikes to reach contralateral CA3 PCs through the VHC was 2.5 ± 0.1 ms (n = 6), and the shortest lag for direct CA3 to contralateral CA1 driving through commissural pathway was 5.8 ± 0.3 ms (n = 7), which is three-fold the L-R lag for spontaneous paired waves.
evaluation: Claims C48-C49 provide critical timing constraints from evoked potential measurements that help interpret the mechanisms of bilateral synchronization. The measurements are straightforward and the sample sizes are adequate (n=6 and n=7). These findings argue against direct contralateral driving as the primary mechanism for most bilateral waves.

result: On average, Schaffer waves led in anterior sites (L: 0.52 ± 0.06 ms, R: 0.67 ± 0.33 ms; F(1,12) = 0.3, p=0.6), but this varied with wave duration. When anterior waves were longer, the a-p lag increased to 2.6 ± 0.3 ms (R) and 2.2 ± 0.3 ms (L) (F(1,12) = 102, p<0.001). When posterior waves were longer, they preceded anterior ones by 1.13 ± 0.5 ms (R) and 1.8 ± 0.3 ms (L) (F(1,12) = 53, p<0.001).
evaluation: Claims C50-C52 demonstrate complex antero-posterior dynamics that depend on wave duration, suggesting independent ignition of CA3 assemblies with variable projection patterns. The statistical tests are appropriate and highly significant, and the findings are consistent with the proposed model of multiple independent CA3 assemblies.

result: CA3som activity showed significant antero-posterior coherence above 25 Hz but no significant bilateral coherence. Cross-correlation coefficients were higher for a-p (0.66 ± 0.6) than L-R comparisons (0.27 ± 0.02; F(1,12) = 32, p<0.001). Amplitude covariance was stronger within (ρA = 0.62 ± 0.06) than between hemispheres (ρA = 0.24 ± 0.04; F(1,14) = 42, p<0.001), with no bilateral amplitude difference (F(1,10) = 0.32, p=0.58). R-waves led by 0.34 ± 0.1 ms (n = 8).
evaluation: Claims C55-C60 characterize CA3som bilateral relationships showing predominantly ipsilateral organization with weak bilateral coupling. The statistical tests are appropriate, sample sizes are stated, and the findings are internally consistent. This contrasts with Schaffer activity and suggests different functional roles.

result: Spectral coherence between CA3som and Schaffer activities was significant only in the gamma band. Cross-correlation was moderate (0.4 ± 0.02, τmax = 4.72 ± 0.4 ms). Granger Causality indicated significant reciprocal relationship peaking in gamma, with CA3som to Schaffer link dominating. Phase analysis showed CA3som leading by Δϕ = 1.46 ± 0.18 radians (Δt = 6.18 ± 0.7 ms), consistent with τmax from cross-correlation.
evaluation: Claims C61-C65 establish the temporal relationship between CA3som and Schaffer activities using multiple analytical approaches that converge on consistent findings. The CA3som precedence is well-established, though the moderate cross-correlation suggests complex relationships. Sample size is adequate (n=12 for GC analysis).

result: The amplitude co-variation between paired Schaffer and CA3som gamma waves was poor (ρA = 0.16 ± 0.02), and the time lag between paired waves was not significant (0.12 ± 0.3 ms). 42.3 ± 2% of CA3som waves remained unpaired with Schaffer waves.
evaluation: Claims C66-C68 reveal important dissociations between CA3som and Schaffer wave features despite their temporal coupling. The poor amplitude covariation and high proportion of unpaired CA3som waves suggest different spatial organization or functional roles. The quantitative measurements are precise and the findings are clearly stated.

result: CA1 pyramidal cells fired preferentially upon convergence of bilateral gamma waves, while putative interneurons showed marked unilateral drive. Interneurons exhibited tight phase-locked firing shortly after bilateral wave onset and fired more frequently than PCs in response to unilateral waves on the same side.
evaluation: Claims C69-C72 demonstrate differential responses of CA1 cell types to bilateral versus unilateral input, supported by data in Figure 5 and supplementary figures. The findings are biologically plausible and consistent with known properties of pyramidal cells and interneurons. However, the exact number of cells analyzed is not clearly stated in these claims.

result: The coincidence of bilateral waves plays a crucial role in PC firing, while the associated power increase has a marginal effect.
evaluation: Claim C73 is supported by analysis of PC firing probability versus Schaffer power (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), which shows that bilateral convergence rather than increased power drives PC firing. This is an important mechanistic insight, though the statistical details of this analysis could be more explicit.

result: Following lidocaine injection in the VHC, Schaffer gamma strings were still observed bilaterally, but frequent unilateral strings occurred that were not seen in controls. Overall power and wave characteristics did not change, indicating autonomous gamma generation by each CA3. Bilateral co-modulation was reduced (CC: 0.62 ± 0.03 vs 0.45 ± 0.05; p=0.007, n=4), bilateral gamma coherence was lost, and L-R synchrony of individual waves disappeared while amplitude variability remained high.
evaluation: Claims C74-C80 provide strong evidence for autonomous bilateral gamma generators through VHC disruption experiments. The findings are internally consistent and well-controlled (evoked potentials confirmed blockade). However, the sample size is relatively small (n=4 animals), and the authors acknowledge potential incomplete blockade of dorso-caudal CA3 fibers through the fimbria.

result: Bilateral excitatory Schaffer gamma waves are generally larger and lead from the right hemisphere with moderate amplitude covariation, drive CA1 pyramidal units more strongly than unilateral waves, and CA3 waves lock to ipsilateral Schaffer potentials with weak bilateral coherence. Schaffer activity may run laterally after pathway disruption. Asymmetric operations promote bilateral entrainment of CA3-autonomous gamma oscillators, synchronizing lateralized gamma strings to converge optimally on CA1 targets, supporting the view that interhippocampal connections integrate different aspects of information flowing through left and right lobes.
evaluation: Claims C3-C9 represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing findings from multiple experimental approaches. These conclusions are well-supported by the detailed quantitative analyses presented in the results section (claims C23-C80). The integration of findings from coherence analysis, wave feature analysis, Granger Causality, unit recording, and VHC disruption provides strong converging evidence.

result: The primacy of the right lobe is supported by multiple lines of evidence: (a) mean lag between paired bilateral waves shows ~0.6-0.8 ms advance on the right; (b) mean amplitude of Schaffer waves was 30% larger on the right; (c) CA3som waves showed similar right-side advance; (d) cumulated lag in crossed comparisons matches partial lags. The short mean lag indicates fine adjustment to optimize temporal overlap of bilateral excitatory envelopes.
evaluation: Claims C81-C83 synthesize multiple lines of evidence for right-side dominance discussed in the Discussion section. The evidence is strong and internally consistent across different measures (timing, amplitude, multiple analytical approaches). The functional interpretation about optimizing temporal overlap is reasonable given the data.

result: The minimum time for CA3 spikes to reach contralateral CA3 PCs (2.5 ms) plus synaptic integration time is insufficient to explain most paired wave lags. Direct contralateral driving of CA1 gamma waves via commissural fibers is unlikely based on: (a) commissural evoked potential lag is in the higher range of spontaneous bilateral wave lags; (b) commissural pathway contributes little to field potentials; (c) presence of unilateral waves; (d) VHC disruption or unilateral CA3 inactivation does not reduce Schaffer waves or power. The most likely origin is independent ipsilateral driving.
evaluation: Claims C84-C86 present a critical mechanistic argument based on timing constraints and multiple lines of evidence. The reasoning is sound and the evidence is strong, though the authors acknowledge that unilateral CA3 assemblies driving contralateral ones cannot be entirely ruled out. The conclusion of independent ipsilateral driving is the most parsimonious explanation.

result: Once every gamma cycle, a collection of spatial modules of CA1 dendritic space is activated over the septo-temporal axis by multiple independent CA3 assemblies with either dominant lamellar or longitudinal projection, converging with others from the contralateral side.
evaluation: Claim C87 presents a conceptual model synthesized from the experimental findings and illustrated in Figure 7. While this is an interpretive model rather than direct observation, it is well-supported by the data on variable antero-posterior dynamics, bilateral convergence patterns, and the presence of multiple independent assemblies. The model is consistent with known hippocampal anatomy.

result: CA3som gamma wavelets are tightly locked to ipsilateral Schaffer waves and arise from basket cell-mediated recurrent inhibition following CA3 PC firing. CA3som activity participates mainly in ipsilateral mechanisms, as indicated by large ipsilateral coherence and nearly synchronous occurrence at anterior and posterior sites, consistent with reported coupling of inhibitory cell subnetworks.
evaluation: Claims C88-C91 synthesize findings on CA3som relationships and propose a mechanistic interpretation. The tight ipsilateral locking and weak bilateral coupling are well-established by the data. The interpretation about basket cell-mediated inhibition is supported by timing relationships and citations to previous work, though direct evidence for basket cell involvement is not provided in this study.

result: The poor covariation between CA3som and Schaffer waves does not support the view that somatic inhibitory input selects the CA3 domain from which functional assemblies arise. An alternative possibility is that multiple CA3 assemblies share a common domain, since nearby PC cells rarely fire together.
evaluation: Claims C92-C93 present an interpretation of the poor amplitude covariation finding (C66). The reasoning is sound and the alternative hypothesis is supported by citations to previous studies on PC firing patterns. However, this remains speculative and would require additional experiments to test directly.

result: Blockade of contralateral CA3 input modifies individual unit firing rates but changes are balanced at the population level. The two CA3-originated excitations in CA1 units do not operate as a simple integrator; rather, output is defined on a single cell basis in concert with other inputs including inhibitory neurons.
evaluation: Claims C99-C100 are supported by data from CA3 blockade experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) and citations to previous studies showing similar population balance. The interpretation about non-linear integration is reasonable given the data, though the mechanisms remain to be fully elucidated.

result: The dominance of the right CA3 may constitute a physiological mechanism for fast bilateral synchronization and stabilization of autonomous CA3 gamma oscillators despite strong amplitude variability. The main functional role for CA3 gamma oscillations may be bilateral entrainment rather than transmitting gamma activity to cortex.
evaluation: Claims C106-C107 present functional hypotheses based on the experimental findings. While speculative, these interpretations are well-grounded in the data showing right-side dominance, autonomous bilateral generators, and the lack of gamma pattern in subicular projections (C104). The hypotheses are testable and provide a framework for understanding the findings.

result: Background and motivation: Lateralization of neural functions bears evolutionary advantages, but bilateral hippocampal function is largely unknown. Important bilateral connections exist between hippocampal subregions. Hippocampal lateralization is observed in rodents during memory tasks, synaptic plasticity, and environmental enrichment, and in humans during sequence disambiguation and cognitive navigation. The CA3 region is an important hub whose output is conveyed to numerous brain regions after bilateral integration in CA1. The left and right CA3 are connected through the VHC and send excitatory inputs to CA1 bilaterally through the Schaffer-commissural system. The CA3 behaves as a powerful gamma oscillator.
evaluation: Claims C10-C22 establish the background and motivation for the study through citations to previous literature. These claims are well-supported by appropriate references and establish the anatomical and functional context for the experimental work. This is standard background material that frames the research questions.

result: Additional background from literature: CA3som generator is part of a gamma pacemaker. Gamma oscillations form rapidly from small clusters of interconnected cells. Coding is optimized by global oscillations with sparse unit firing. Gamma rhythmic CA3 input implies chunked information. Connection asymmetry favors temporal association. Different hippocampal subregions are differentially involved in encoding/consolidation of spatial information. Spatial and non-spatial information converge in hippocampus to form episodic memories. Both CA3 are required for short-term memory, but only left CA3 inactivation impairs long-term spatial memory. The hippocampus represents behavioral episodes as sequences of events.
evaluation: Claims C53, C95-C97, C105, C110-C112, and C114 provide additional background from literature that contextualizes the findings. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to previous work. This background material helps interpret the functional significance of the experimental findings.

result: Speculative interpretations and hypotheses: Both CA3 PCs and basket cells may receive common tonic input coding for gamma string duration as an energy-saving mechanism. Information conveyed may be similar or different on both sides in different epochs. PC firing dispersion may arise from slower EPSP dynamics and/or variable interneuron influence. Some interneurons may act as timing devices. Gamma-phase shifting of CA1-PCs indicates short-lived gamma pattern restricted to CA3-CA1 segment. Larger right-side Schaffer waves may reflect glutamate receptor asymmetry or larger CA3 assemblies. Right dominance fits a hardware-like role for integrating lateralized information streams. Left and right sides do not convey equivalent information. CA3 assemblies may sequentially code scene features in gamma strings that are checked bilaterally. This mechanism may subserve bilateral assemblage in other brain structures.
evaluation: Claims C94, C98, C101-C103, C108-C109, C113, C115-C116 present various speculative interpretations and hypotheses. While these are grounded in the experimental findings and supported by relevant citations, they remain speculative and would require additional experiments to test directly. Some are more plausible than others based on the available evidence.
